questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify the job of a working definition placed before its first use
questions.stem: A technical book opens a section with one sentence: "In this book, dormancy means an organism's metabolism slowing to a halt for a season, not pausing briefly." The next ten paragraphs use the word throughout. What does that opening sentence do for the reader?

options.text: It fixes the sense of the term before the argument leans on it
It reports that specialists disagree about how to use the term
options.misconception: reads a flat definition as a report of disagreement in the field

options.text: It states the section's main conclusion before any evidence is given
options.misconception: takes a definition for a premature announcement of the conclusion

options.text: It tells the reader which of the author's claims to doubt first
options.misconception: assumes a definition functions as a signal of doubt about the claim

questions.explanation: A technical term should be fixed before the first sentence that depends on it, because every later use hands its meaning to whatever sense the reader took away. This book defines dormancy in its opening line and then leans on the word for ten paragraphs, so the definition is not decoration but the ground the section stands on. The tempting reading treats the opening as a warning that the field uses the word loosely, yet nothing in the sentence reports any variation in usage, and the definition is given flatly, the way a book settles its own usage rather than reporting someone else's.
questions.hint: Ask what the following ten paragraphs have to rely on.

questions.learningObjective: explain what an attributed evaluative phrase does inside an integrated quotation
questions.stem: A paragraph runs: "The 1988 survey reported what its compilers called a decisive shift: only twelve of ninety libraries kept the maps on open shelves." The next sentence spends itself showing why that count proves less than it appears to. What work does the phrase "what its compilers called a decisive shift" do?

options.text: It presents the compilers' judgment as the writer's own unargued claim
options.misconception: misses that the evaluation is attributed and then disputed

options.text: It borrows the compilers' word and flags that the writer will contest it
It supplies a second measurement that corroborates the figure of twelve
options.misconception: reads a label on one number as a second piece of evidence

options.text: It substitutes a paraphrase for the compilers' exact wording in the source
options.misconception: assumes a framing phrase displaces a quotation that should appear

questions.explanation: Integrating a source means naming whose judgment is being imported and then saying what the writer does with it. "What its compilers called" marks the evaluative words as the compilers' property, and the sentence that follows, showing the count proves less than it appears to, is the author's contest. Together they leave the evaluation visible and disputable instead of laundering it into the writer's own voice. The tempting reading hears a colon and assumes the words after it belong to the writer, which is exactly the theft of voice the attribution clause exists to prevent.
questions.hint: Ask who owns the word "decisive" in that paragraph.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: state the end-weight principle that governs sentence ordering
questions.stem: Two sentences carry one fact. "The battery lost twelve per cent of its capacity in the first winter." "In the first winter, the battery lost twelve per cent of its capacity." What does the ordering of the second sentence do?

options.text: It places the quantity the reader must keep at the sentence's end
It shows that the loss grew more severe during that first winter
options.misconception: reads a change of word order as a change in the size of the loss

options.text: It marks the first sentence as informal and the second as formal
options.misconception: treats reordering as a shift of register rather than of emphasis

options.text: It signals that the figure is an estimate rather than a measurement
options.misconception: hears a restatement as a claim about the figure's precision

questions.explanation: Readers retain what a sentence ends on, so an author who wants a figure remembered gives it the last position. In the second version the quantity, twelve per cent, closes the line while the date that qualifies it opens, and the information a reader might dispute ends up where doubt is least likely to start. The tempting reading hears a change of word order as a change of tone, as though one version were casual and the other formal; no diction has changed, and the second is not more exact, only better placed for the memory it needs to serve.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: locate a delayed controlling idea and judge whether the delay earns its place
questions.stem: Three sentences of a report's paragraph give background: the archive opened in 1974, the collection was catalogued by hand, and the first catalogue listed 3,200 boxes. The fourth sentence begins, "The scale of that effort is what makes the omissions telling." Where is this paragraph's controlling idea?

options.text: In the fourth sentence, after the detail that gives the point its force
In the first sentence, which sets the archive's history for the reader
options.misconception: credits the opening background sentence with the paragraph's claim

options.text: Nowhere, because a paragraph must announce its point in its opening line
options.misconception: treats any delayed controlling idea as a structural error

options.text: In the second sentence, where the difficulty of the work is first implied
options.misconception: locates the claim in an implication rather than in a stated sentence

questions.explanation: A controlling idea can be stated late when the evidence that gives it force has to arrive first, because a reader who is handed the claim before the scale of the cataloguing exists has nothing to measure it against. Here the fourth sentence does two jobs at once: it names the point and it converts 3,200 boxes from a fact into a measure of the gaps. The tempting reading holds that a paragraph's job is to announce itself at once, and it is right about clearer paragraphs, but it misses that a point stated before its own grounds is an assertion rather than an explanation.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: sequence a mechanism so that each step produces the next
questions.stem: A student must explain in one paragraph why a footpath floods after a storm. She has four materials: the amount of rain a single storm delivers, the soil's saturation capacity, a gully at the bottom of the path that is blocked with leaf litter, and advice about walking in rain. Put the four in the order she should use them.

answer.exemplar: She should begin with the rain, because nothing else in the chain can begin without it, since a storm that delivers less than the soil can hold never causes a flood; then the soil's capacity, which is the point at which the water has nowhere left to go; then the blocked gully, which is the reason that overflow stands on the path rather than running off it; and close with the advice, which is the one thing a reader can act on and which only makes sense once the mechanism is visible.

questions.explanation: A mechanism is a chain of causes, so the order has to run from the condition that starts the process to the consequence a reader can act on, with each item producing the item after it. The rain fills the soil, the soil's capacity is what it can take, and the blocked gully is why the surplus stays where it is, so those three form one another in that order. The tempting reading starts with the advice or the dates, on the grounds that a reader wants the conclusion first, but a conclusion that arrives before the process explains is a rule to obey rather than a reason to understand.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four is a cause of the next, and which is a use of the whole.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify the sentences that mark the reach of the evidence
questions.stem: A paragraph about a new bridge coating makes five assertions. Three of them mark how far its evidence actually reaches. Which are those three?

options.text: The coating appears to double the interval between repaints in one trial
The coating's benefits have been demonstrated in laboratories worldwide
options.misconception: states a bare generalisation where the testing was local

options.text: Two laboratories tested the coating, and suggest the figure is conservative
The council's inspection regime has not changed since the coating went on
options.misconception: reads a plain contextual fact as a limitation of the evidence

options.text: No published study has tested the coating in freezing conditions

questions.explanation: Calibration shows the reader where the evidence stops, and it does that in three recognisable ways: marking how firm the claim is, using a verb weaker than proof, and naming the conditions nobody has tested. This paragraph reports a single trial, says two laboratories suggest the figure is conservative, and records that freezing conditions are untested, so each sentence marks a limit. The tempting reading treats any measured-sounding sentence as calibrated, but the claim about laboratories worldwide and the note about the inspection regime are both unmarked assertions, and one of them widens the evidence well past what any source in the paragraph supplies.
questions.hint: Ask which sentences would survive being quoted against the writer.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: define what makes a group of sentences one paragraph
questions.stem: A paragraph opens "Most metals expand when they are heated," gives four examples, and closes that expansion is small enough for engineers to correct. What makes these sentences one paragraph rather than five?

options.text: They all serve one idea, and each sentence does a job for it
They share a subject, since a metal is named in every sentence
options.misconception: equates a common topic with a paragraph's controlling idea

options.text: They run in the order in which the events being described happened
options.misconception: explains a paragraph by chronology rather than by purpose

options.text: They were written together, and the paragraph is only a unit of writing
options.misconception: treats the physical act of composition as the thing that binds sentences

questions.explanation: A paragraph is a set of sentences under one controlling idea, with each sentence doing a job for that idea rather than merely sitting near it. Here the claim about expansion is stated, the four examples test it, and the closing sentence gives it a consequence, so nothing in the paragraph could be lifted out without leaving a hole. The tempting reading offers a shared subject or a shared stretch of writing, and both are true of many sets of sentences that are not paragraphs at all, since a page of notes about metals can share every one of those features and still argue nothing.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence would leave a hole if it were cut.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish synthesis from single-source report
questions.stem: Sentence A: "Bond's 1962 survey of forty libraries found nine with open-shelf maps." Sentence B: "Across the surveys of that decade, open-shelf maps sat in a small minority of libraries, so the practice was a specialist habit rather than a regional norm." Which does B do that A cannot?

options.text: It reports the survey's own conclusion about what the maps meant
options.misconception: attributes a generalisation to a source that only counted

options.text: It draws a generalisation across sources rather than reporting one survey
It names how many libraries took part in the counting
options.misconception: thinks a generalisation should also supply a headcount

options.text: It explains why the maps were kept closed on the library shelves
options.misconception: reads a pattern in practice as a motive for the practice

questions.explanation: Reporting tells a reader what one source found; synthesising tells a reader what several sources add up to, and only the second can support a claim about a practice rather than about a survey. B ranges across the decade's surveys and infers a norm, which the forty libraries in A could not have shown however large the count. The tempting reading wants B to be A's conclusion, since 'so the practice was a specialist habit' sounds like a verdict the survey might have delivered; but a survey of forty libraries reporting nine is a fact about that survey, and the habit it documents is a claim about the decade.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: choose the integration that holds a single claim together
questions.stem: A student must support one claim: "The 1990s move to closed stacks was a budget decision, not a security decision." She has Source 1, the minutes of a 1993 committee, recording the sum allocated to security staff, and Source 2, a librarian's 2004 memoir, describing the galleries emptying and blaming cost-cutting. options.misconception: prefers vivid testimony to documentary evidence on a claim about money

options.text: Use the minutes alone, because a committee record outranks any later account
options.misconception: treats a genre's rank as a substitute for showing a consequence

options.text: Quote both without comment, letting the reader see which one shows a budget
options.misconception: believes juxtaposition is the same as integration

options.text: Use the minutes for the money, the memoir for the emptying galleries, and mark the memoir's blame as opinion

questions.learningObjective: state what a signpost tells a skimming reader
questions.stem: Halfway down a paragraph a sentence reads, "This is where the evidence gets thin." What does that sentence do for a reader who is skimming?

options.misconception: hears a limit as a promise of better evidence later

The tempting reading hears the word 'thin' as a remark about the writing or as a summary, and neither is possible here: the sentence sits at the midpoint, promises nothing better later, and names a property of evidence rather than of sentences.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: recognise cumulative structure and distinguish it from causal attribution
questions.stem: A paragraph runs: "The filter clogged. The pressure rose. The pump failed. The wing was shut down for eleven days." What kind of structure holds these sentences together?

options.text: Additive, since each sentence contributes an equal fact on the same level
options.misconception: misses that each sentence makes the next one unavoidable

options.text: Cumulative, since each sentence adds a consequence the one before requires
Causal, since each sentence supplies the cause of the event named next
options.misconception: credits the chain with a claim about cause the paragraph never makes

options.text: Illustrative, since the sentences show a general rule in specific cases
options.misconception: reads a sequence of events as an instance of a stated rule

questions.explanation: A cumulative paragraph builds by addition, each sentence putting one more consequence on the pile so that the reader reaches the end having watched the total grow. Here clogging, pressure, failure, and eleven days of grounding are not four facts at one level but four rungs, and the last is only intelligible because the three before it have happened. The tempting reading wants the sequence named causal, and the distinction matters: a cumulative chain shows what followed what and lets the reader draw the causal line, whereas a causal paragraph would have to say which of these produced the shutdown, which this one never does.
questions.hint: Ask whether the last sentence would be true if the first had not happened.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: explain the function of a framing clause before a quotation
questions.stem: A writer introduces a quotation: "The old guard, as the 1974 pamphlet put it, wanted the collection closed until it could be properly catalogued." What does the framing clause accomplish?

options.misconception: assumes attribution alone removes the writer from a judgment

options.text: It tells the reader whose words these are before the quoted words arrive
It explains the pamphlet's argument so the reader need not follow it
options.misconception: treats a signpost as a substitute for the source's own content

options.text: It reports how widely the pamphlet's phrase was borrowed afterwards
options.misconception: infers a borrowing history from a single attributed phrase

The tempting reading believes the frame is a disclaimer that clears the writer of the sentence's content, but the writer chose that pamphlet and chose to quote that phrase, so attribution locates the opinion without excusing the choice of it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: explain the framing a quotation needs inside an arguing paragraph
questions.stem: A writer plans to set a forty-word quotation into the middle of a sixty-word paragraph. Explain what she must supply around it, and what she must keep, so that the paragraph still argues something once the quotation is in place.

answer.exemplar: She must supply a sentence before the quotation that says what the quotation is being enlisted for, and a sentence after it that returns to the claim, because a quotation that arrives without a job becomes the paragraph. She must keep the writer's own claim and the qualification attached to it, even if the quotation is the better prose, since the argument and not the evidence is what the section is for.

questions.explanation: A quotation is evidence inside a claim, so it needs a job and an aftermath: the sentence that introduces it must say what it is doing for the argument, and the sentence that follows must put the reader back on the claim. Cutting those two leaves a paragraph that is forty words of someone else's voice and twenty words of the writer's, which reads as an illustration rather than an argument. The tempting reading believes the best sentence should simply be the most vivid one, and in isolation it often is, but a paragraph that surrenders its claim to a quotation has stopped arguing and started displaying.
questions.hint: Ask what the quotation is for, and where the reader lands after it.

questions.learningObjective: state what a paragraph commits its writer to after an opening sentence

Listing all four closures with the date of each in turn

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: detect a quantifier that widens between two sentences
questions.stem: A paragraph reads, "Some of the earliest maps were kept behind glass. Early maps were therefore kept behind glass." What happens between the two sentences?

options.text: The evidence is introduced, and the conclusion is then drawn from it
options.misconception: reads a change of quantifier as ordinary inference

options.text: The quantifier weakens to nothing, and a limited record becomes a general rule
The writer concedes a limitation, and then answers the objection
options.misconception: reads 'some' as a concession rather than as a quantifier

options.text: The first sentence is withdrawn, so the second states what is left
options.misconception: treats a hedge as a retraction of the earlier claim

'Some of the earliest maps' reports a portion with no proportion attached, so the second sentence, which leaves out the quantifier and reaches all early maps, has drawn a general rule from an unsized portion. The tempting reading sees evidence first and conclusion second and calls the pair sound, which is the mistake: a conclusion is licensed by the strength of what precedes it, and dropping the word 'some' is not a conclusion, it is a different claim with no evidence behind it.

questions.learningObjective: identify sentences that can be tightened without losing information
questions.stem: A paragraph contains five sentences. Three of them can be tightened without losing anything a reader needs. Which are those three?

The sample was drawn from two schools in one district
options.misconception: treats the sample's limits as though they were padding

The report had predicted a failure date of the following March
options.misconception: cuts the only sentence that dates the prediction

questions.learningObjective: state the job of a bridge sentence between two sources
questions.stem: A writer has quoted a 1974 pamphlet and then a 1990 census of holdings, and has one sentence left to join them into a single point. Explain what that sentence has to do, and what it must leave alone.

It must leave the two sources' separate wording alone, because the value of the pair lies in their difference of vantage, and it must not rank them, since nothing in the material makes one more authoritative than the other.

questions.explanation: A bridge sentence is where integration actually happens, and it earns its place by naming the relation between the two sources rather than by summarising them again. An intention recorded in 1974 and a count taken in 1990 can be joined by a single claim about practice, and that claim is the writer's own, not either source's. The tempting reading uses the sentence to settle which source is right, since a writer feels obliged to adjudicate, but adjudication is a different job with different evidence; a bridge that ranks two sources has quietly stopped integrating and started judging, and the claim it was meant to carry is left unsaid.

questions.stem: A report states, "Eighty per cent of the repairs failed within five years." The same report gives the number of repairs carried out each year. What does that sentence leave a reader without?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: repair a percentage that has lost its denominator
questions.stem: A sentence states: "The scheme cut missed appointments by 75 per cent." A footnote says the baseline was 40,000 appointments a year. Explain what must be added for the claim to be usable, and what must not be.

answer.exemplar: It must be given the baseline and the period, so the reader can see that 75 per cent of 40,000 appointments is thirty thousand a year, and so that the reader can tell an annual figure from a cumulative one. questions.explanation: A percentage is a claim about a ratio, and a ratio is only usable when the reader knows both terms and the period over which they were counted. Adding the baseline converts the sentence from an impressive magnitude into a weight the reader can picture. The tempting reading supplies a cause, because a large improvement invites an explanation, and adds a forecast because readers always want to know next year; both would be new claims with no evidence behind them, and a sentence repaired for use must not quietly acquire a second and untested assertion.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader needs in order to picture the number, and what they are not entitled to.

questions.learningObjective: state what a parenthetical contributes and what it protects

options.misconception: treats a parenthesis as a new topic

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: choose the summary that preserves a source's scope and share
questions.stem: A source reports: "Among the 300 households we surveyed, none had replaced a boiler in the last five years; 62 per cent gave cost as the main reason they had not." Which one-sentence version keeps the finding intact?

options.text: Most households named cost as the main reason for not replacing a boiler
options.misconception: turns a 62 per cent share into a majority and loses the sample

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify the work done by a signalled surprise
questions.stem: A paragraph states a finding and then adds, "This is surprising, since the two groups had identical training." What work does the final clause do?

options.misconception: treats a surprise clause as a proof

options.text: It concedes that the groups were in fact better trained
options.misconception: inverts a statement of equal training into a concession

options.text: It supplies the expectation the finding breaks, so it can be felt as one
It hints that the finding is too good to be believed
options.misconception: reads a signalled surprise as a signal of unreliability

'Since the two groups had identical training' supplies that expectation in six words, and the reader can then measure the result against it. The tempting reading treats the clause as proof, as though removing an obvious explanation settled the question; it does not, since a result can defeat an expectation and still have another explanation, and the clause is doing the work of setting up a comparison, not closing one.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader needed to believe in order to feel surprised.

questions.learningObjective: identify the sentences that add nothing to a reader's understanding

The supplier has since apologised in writing and offered to re-stock
options.misconception: cuts the only record of what the supplier did afterwards

The part was ordered on 4 March and arrived on 25 March
options.misconception: treats the only dated evidence as though it were repetition

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: predict which element a rewrite emphasises
questions.stem: A writer rewrites "In the three districts we studied, waiting times fell" as "Waiting times fell in the three districts we studied." What does the rewrite emphasise?

The three districts, which a general reader is likelier to forget

options.misconception: assumes that reordering cannot change emphasis

options.misconception: confuses emphasis with evidentiary weight

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: choose a revision that front-loads a purpose without changing the fact
questions.stem: A methods paragraph reads, "Packing the boxes in ice kept the sample cool." Which revision improves the emphasis without changing the meaning?

options.misconception: reverses who packs what and changes the procedure

options.text: To keep the sample cool, the boxes were packed in ice

options.misconception: turns a report of a procedure into advice to the reader

options.misconception: shifts the tense and leaves the procedure unperformed

questions.hint: Ask which version still reports what happened.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify what a repeated sentence opening accumulates
questions.stem: A paragraph opens four sentences the same way: "The first survey asked...", "The first survey found...", "The first survey missed...", "The first survey was never repeated..." What does the repetition do?

options.misconception: credits anaphora with economy rather than with emphasis

options.text: It shows the writer has run out of ways to begin a sentence
options.misconception: reads deliberate repetition as stylistic exhaustion

options.text: It holds one subject in view while four claims accumulate against it
It divides the four claims into four separate paragraphs
options.misconception: confuses repeated openings with structural division

questions.explanation: When every sentence starts the same way, the reader's attention stays on the repeated element while the rest of each sentence changes, and here that element is the same survey doing four different things: asking, finding, missing, and never being repeated. The effect is accumulation against a fixed subject, which is a way of building a verdict out of four modest facts. The tempting reading calls the repetition economical, and it does save words, but the words it saves are not the work it does; the work is the pressure of four charges against one name.
questions.hint: Ask what stays constant across the four sentences.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: write a limitation that narrows a claim without withdrawing it
questions.stem: A writer's claim is that a street redesign cut pedestrian injuries. One figure in the supporting evidence comes from a hospital two towns away. Explain how to write that limitation in a sentence that keeps the claim standing.

answer.exemplar: The sentence should say which part of the evidence the distance affects and leave the rest alone, for instance that the hospital's records cover a different catchment and so confirm the direction of the fall without fixing its size for this street. It must not generalise the figure to the street, and it must not turn a boundary in the evidence into a doubt about the redesign, since a claim that survives its own limits is worth more than one that never met any.

questions.explanation: A limitation is not an apology, and the sentence that states one works best when it separates the part of the evidence the problem touches from the part it leaves standing. A hospital two towns away confirms a direction and cannot fix a local rate, and a reader told that can still use the figure for the claim the paragraph is making. The tempting reading writes the limitation as a hedge over the whole claim, on the reasonable ground that honesty should be visible; but a hedge that covers the claim withdraws the thing it was supposed to qualify, and the writer is left apologising for evidence that is still doing work.
questions.hint: Ask which half of the evidence the problem touches.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify what a parallel structure contributes to emphasis
questions.stem: A sentence uses a repeated structure to land three refusals: "Not faster, not cheaper, not safer." What does the parallel form do?

options.misconception: reads parallelism as a logical conjunction

options.text: It makes the three refusals arrive as one weight rather than three
It removes the need to say what is being refused
options.misconception: assumes the form carries the content unaided

options.text: It makes the sentence easier to translate into other languages
options.misconception: credits parallelism with translation rather than with emphasis

questions.explanation: Parallel structure puts several items in the same grammatical slot so that a reader meets them in the same rhythm and adds their weights instead of setting them side by side. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify the claim a causal rewrite adds to correlational evidence
questions.stem: A report states, "In districts where the water plant was upgraded, stomach illness fell 40 per cent." A draft of the same report reads, "Upgrading the plant cut stomach illness by 40 per cent." What does the rewrite claim that the evidence does not?

options.text: That the illness fell, which the data show in either version
options.misconception: confuses the direction of a change with a claim about its cause

options.text: That the upgrade caused the fall, rather than the two moving together
That the upgrade was worth doing, which follows from the size of the fall
options.misconception: reads a causal claim as a verdict on value

options.text: That untreated districts got worse, which the comparison must imply
options.misconception: invents a counterfactual the passage never states

questions.explanation: 'In districts where' and 'upgrading' do different work: the first reports a co-occurrence, and the second makes the upgrade the agent of the result, which is a claim about cause and opens a question the data cannot answer. That a plant was upgraded somewhere and illness fell there does not tell us what would have happened without the upgrade. The tempting reading accepts the causal version because the rewrite is more concise, and it is true that agency makes a sentence shorter; but concision here is being bought with an inference, and the rewrite would remain a better sentence if it said the two moved together.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would need in order to say the plant caused it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: sequence connectors by how far each one moves the reader
questions.stem: A writer has three connectors available for a paragraph, and each one hands the reader on a different distance. Place them in the order of that distance: from the connector that keeps the reader inside the clause being written to the one that hands the reader to a later part of the section.

options.text: Such as, which adds a case inside the clause being written
options.misconception: treats an in-clause case as the connector a paragraph opens with

options.text: For example, which opens a case in the next sentence of this paragraph
options.misconception: sends the reader out of the paragraph as soon as a case is added

options.text: Which raises the question the next section will take up
options.misconception: keeps the reader inside the paragraph when the connector hands them onward

questions.learningObjective: state what a sentence offering two explanations has established
questions.stem: A sentence offers two explanations: "The delay came either from the failed delivery or from the missing paperwork." What has the sentence established?

questions.learningObjective: resolve a pronoun in a sentence that carries a report
questions.stem: Two consecutive sentences read: "The 1974 report counted 3,200 boxes. Most of them were never consulted, the auditors found." What does "them" refer to?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: explain when a late controlling idea is a strength
questions.stem: A paragraph withholds its point until the last sentence, and the last sentence lands well. Explain why a reader accepts this, and what the writer would lose by moving the point to the front.

answer.exemplar: The reader accepts it because each earlier sentence has been doing the last sentence's work: naming a cost, a time, and an alternative gives the closing claim something to land on, and a claim the reader has already been given the grounds for reads as a conclusion rather than an instruction. Moving the point to the front would keep the clarity and lose the pressure, since a reader told the point first has nothing left to be surprised by and will read the rest as evidence they have already been given.

questions.explanation: A late controlling idea works when the sentences before it are the grounds for it, because the reader arrives at the last sentence holding the very facts the claim depends on and can feel the claim as a result. A front-loaded point is clearer but flatter: the reader is told what to think before they have anything to think with, and the paragraph becomes an illustration of a conclusion already settled. The tempting reading treats a late point as a fault of structure, and it is a fault when the preceding sentences are not its grounds, in which case the last sentence lands on nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is holding when the last sentence arrives.
